summary:
Omsk Oblast is one of the federal subjects of the Russian Federation and stands under the national legal framework. The sources reviewed record no oblast-level divergence in statute, enforcement or protection, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia, version 2.0 of June 2025, carries no oblast-level detail.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised under Russian law, while same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned. Gender-affirming healthcare was effectively prohibited in 2023, and in November 2023 the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation. That designation applies in Omsk Oblast as it does across the federation.

'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals, or up to 15 days' detention. The expanded propaganda provisions reach public expression that justifies gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention and deportation, and the US State Department's advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers.

Participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols is prosecuted as extremism, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 such convictions as of 30 June 2025, and the UK Home Office note records that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded in January 2024, when masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling: about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The capital is cited as a single illustration of national practice rather than as evidence about Omsk.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 the case of a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The incident is recorded in a different oblast and indicates national risk, not an Omsk case.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Protection pathways outside Russia are being set by other governments. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia, and the UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.
localsOnly:
Russian citizens and residents of Omsk Oblast cannot obtain legal gender recognition. The law signed in 2023 prohibits gender reassignment surgery and changes of gender marker on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year.

Same-sex marriage is unavailable, so there is no partner recognition for same-sex couples.

Displaying banned LGBT symbols is an administrative offence under article 20.3. Human Rights Watch documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024, most of them for material posted on social media.

Participation in the designated 'international LGBT movement' or display of its symbols is charged as extremism and carries up to 12 years in prison; 101 convictions had been issued by 30 June 2025. The national figure of at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024 is recorded without a federal-subject breakdown, so the oblast's share is not itemised.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source reviewed records Omsk-specific enforcement. The UK Home Office note carries no oblast-level detail, and neither the extremism conviction tally nor the article 20.3 case counts are broken down by federal subject. Whether Omsk police have conducted bar raids or extremism arrests remains unresolved on this inventory.

The conversion-therapy detention reported by BBC Russian took place near Novosibirsk, in a different oblast. It is presented here as national risk evidence and is not attributable to Omsk Oblast.

The pretrial detention death reported by the Associated Press in December 2024 is not located to a named facility or region in the inventory, so its bearing on Omsk Oblast is unresolved.

Regional bylaws specific to Omsk Oblast on public gatherings, local administrative practice under article 20.3, and any hate-crime enhancement covering gender identity are not sourced here.
